newsitem.title: FRANCE: French railways brace for widespread strike.
newsitem.headline: French railways brace for widespread strike.

text.p: France braced for a 36-hour rail strike from Wednesday and more social unrest loomed as civil service trade unions threatened to strike for wage hikes.

The rail strike against a proposed government reform of the state railways SNCF was officially scheduled to run from midnight on Wednesday to Friday 8 a.m. (0700 GMT), but was expected to start biting from 8 p.m. (1900 GMT) on Wednesday.
SNCF said it could hit up to two-thirds of train services, but Eurostar trains through the Channel Tunnel between Paris and London and high-speed services to Belgium should run normally.

The number of high-speed train services will be cut by half and traffic on the conventional network would be cut by one third in the north and east, and by two thirds elsewhere. Paris commuter trains would be cut by one third to one half.
The strike could prove the most disruptive since 1995 when a stoppage by rail workers spread across the public sector and crippled the country for several weeks in November and December.
Bruno d'Alberto, head of the rail branch at the Socialist CFDT trade union said the action would be a test for possible further protests.
Civil service unions said they would discuss calling a strike after the government announces pay offers next Tuesday.

CGC union leader Pierre Avignon said unofficial contacts with the civil service ministry in the past few days led unions to believe the government was not willing to make any concessions on a "catch-up" after a wage freeze in 1996.
"We're expecting the government's proposals on February 4. It appears now that they won't live up to what we want," he told Reuters.

Avignon said the main unions involved were seeking pay rises of 1.4 percent in 1997 and 1998 and were also looking for at least a gesture from the ministry to make up for the loss of purchasing power in 1996.
The CGC and other unions wanted to negotiate but some of the unions were taking a harder line. Avignon said if a strike were called, it would probably happen in March.
Turnout in the last strike on October 17, to protest against planned job cuts, was relatively modest with one in three civil servants stopping work.
Besides renewed tensions in the civil service and railways, the government also faces protests from urban transport staff.
The southwestern city of Toulouse was disrupted for the third successive day on Wednesday by a bus driver strike to demand shorter working hours and early retirement at 55.

The Confederation Generale des Travailleurs (CGT) and Force Ouvriere (FO) unions have called a nationwide strike on the metro (underground railway), bus and other urban transit systems on February 6 to press similar demands.

Truckers won the right to retire at 55 after blocking roads last year. But the government, on an austerity drive to meet the criteria for the European single currency, says lowering the retirement age to 55 from 60 for everyone is unfeasible.

The Communist-led CGT and Socialist CFDT unions, with a majority of the 180,000 rail staff, have called the strike over a law which they say will break up the SNCF, threatening the rail monopoly, jobs and loss-making railway lines.

Transport Minister Bernard Pons has proposed to create a state holding company to take over 132 billion francs ($23.67 billion) in debt out of more than 200 billion ($35.86 billion) run up mainly in developing the high-speed TGV train system.

The reform law has been passed in the Senate and will go before the National Assembly (lower house) with backing from other unions on grounds that the SNCF would otherwise buckle under its debts and soaring interest payments.
